item.title: AI in Nebraska education: Parents, teachers and students grapple with artificial intelligence in schools
item.description:
# AI in Nebraska education: Parents, teachers and students grapple with artificial intelligence in schools #### Listen To This Story She said she found out Omaha Public Schools, where her daughter is enrolled, uses a fluency-grading AI tool called Amira.
The use of artificial intelligence is growing in classrooms, with national data showing more teachers and students are using it. According to a Center for Democracy & Technology [survey](https://cdt.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024-03-21-CDT-Civic-Tech-Generative-AI-Survey-Research-final.pdf), 83% of teachers reported using ChatGPT or another generative AI tool in the 2023-24 school year. Results from a Pew Research Center [survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/02/24/how-teens-use-and-view-ai/) showed more than half of teenagers say they used an AI chatbot to find information or get help with schoolwork.
She noticed when students were using Grammarly, an AI editing software, they weren’t learning how to properly write.
## **Ethics, inaccuracies raise questions** Jordan Martin, who will start his first year as the high school business teacher at Wilber-Clatonia Public Schools, said artificial intelligence is helping him develop some of his materials, like coming up with wrong answers for multiple-choice questions on tests.
There’s also a systemwide policy on ways faculty can [utilize](https://nebraska.edu/offices/information-technology-services/technology-support/artificial-intelligence/responsible-use#faculty) AI tools, which includes using it to “enhance or improve assignments.”
## **Avoiding artificial intelligence** “Whether it's physical medium or digital or whatever it may be, you're partaking in the act of creation.
“Someone, instead of doing the work themselves, they just typed it into ChatGPT or whatever they used and had it generate all of their looks for them,” Traxler said.

item.title: How artificial intelligence is changing periodontal assessment: Enhancing diagnostic accuracy in dental hygiene practice
item.description:
# How artificial intelligence is changing periodontal assessment: Enhancing diagnostic accuracy in dental hygiene practice Artificial intelligence is transforming periodontal care by helping dental hygienists detect subtle radiographic findings, improve patient education, and support more consistent treatment planning.
## Key Highlights Artificial intelligence is one of the latest advancements reshaping dentistry, and periodontal assessment is an area where it has great potential.
Helping patients understand the seriousness of a condition they cannot see or feel is one of the most difficult yet most important parts of periodontal care. [Artificial intelligence](https://www.rdhmag.com/career-profession/article/55293064/9-things-every-hygienist-should-know-about-dental-ai) offers another tool to support earlier detection, monitor progression, enhance patient education and understanding, and strengthen the periodontal care we provide every day.2

item.title: Experts say artificial intelligence is not coming for your job just yet
item.description:
# Experts say artificial intelligence is not coming for your job just yet AI has been adopted across most industries, but experts say it’s largely playing an assistive role rather than replacing jobs outright.
The increasingly routine use of artificial intelligence in the workplace is virtually undeniable, though experts say there’s no need to panic about it overtaking jobs — at least not yet.
Google’s new AI & Economy ATLAS report, released July 23, finds that AI is mostly playing an assistive role — helping with ideas, strategy and similar tasks — while fully automating work remains rare.
The study, based on 15 million interactions with Google’s AI products including the Gemini app and AI Mode, found that while AI has been adopted across all industry sectors and 68% of all occupations, it is being used selectively and for only approximately 21% of tasks.
“To be able to use it strategically, where it doesn’t seem like they are a robot, but they’re really using it as a resource and a tool.”

UNLV is working to ensure that faculty and its departments are integrating AI training and resources into courses and operations so that students are ahead of the curve, said Moore, whose office offers a resource on using AI collaboratively in job searches.
That doesn’t mean letting AI write your cover letter, Moore made clear, but using it to get tips and tricks on a cover letter based on a job’s description.
Another example, Moore said, is using AI to explore job opportunities — letting it work alongside you instead of overtaking you.
